newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ shrs rally on CPI data to end at 32 month high.
newsitem.headline: NZ shrs rally on CPI data to end at 32 month high.

text.p: The New Zealand share market rose 57.18 points to close at a new 32 month high of 2321.66 on Tuesday after weaker-than-expected CPI data prompted one of the largest rally equities have seen this year, brokers said.
"On memory, it would be the best day this year," said Tim Koller of Hendry Hay McIntosh. "It was totally across the market and it was very solid volume."

Brokers said the market had opened strongly, but the release at 10.45 a.m. (2145 GMT) of CPI data, which put core inflation at 2.4 percent in the September year against expectations of 2.7 percent, had caused a sharp fall in interest rates.
"The bills rallied, and the market took off," Koller said.
Strength in the debt market had contributed to the standout performance of Telecom, which finished 32 cents higher at an all-time high of $7.32.
"For people buying New Zealand, this is the one to buy," Cavill White's Don Turkington said of the market leader, an interest rate-sensitive stock.
Turkington agreed that the good inflation news this morning had "really kicked the market along".
"People are not wanting to sell into this because, especially locally, a lot of people are not heavily weighted in equities," he said.

A plethora of stocks reached new highs for the year: INL was up 20 cents at $6.20, Nuplex was also 20 stronger at $6.00, Fletcher Building rose 17 to $3.82, Sky City was 15 cents firmer at $7.90, Fisher and Paykel gained 15 to $5.25, and Ports of Auckland was up 10 to $5.80, to name just a few.
Reflecting the strength in second-tier stocks, the small companies index was 112.34 points higher at 4,581.02.
"It looks like, for today anyway, the uncertainty associated with the election has been put on hold," said ANZ Securities broker Duncan Rutherford.
Saturday's historic general election under a new proportional system has yet to produce a government, with the main parties currently courting coalition partners.
Rutherford said it was reasonable to assume that profit-takers would enter the market at some stage to take advantage of the gains.
"I would suspect, given that there has been such a strong rise, there would be some profit-taking at some stage," he said
"I guess now it's just a question of when."
